We welcome people interested in astrophysics, orbital mechanics, aerospace engineering, GIS, scientific research and data visualization. If you enjoy exploring ideas and building meaningful solutions together, we'd love to have you on our team!
summary:
LUNA-RESOLVE is a terrain-aware analysis platform that helps explore solar illumination and geometric Earth visibility at candidate lunar south-pole sites. Using NASA lunar elevation data and SPICE-based celestial geometry, it evaluates how local terrain and observer height influence visibility over a 30-day mission window.

The platform analyzes two candidate regions, Nobile Rim 1 and Connecting Ridge, using 1,441 observations per site at 30-minute intervals. Its interactive dashboard presents solar and Earth elevation time series, terrain-modelled solar visibility, Earth-disk visibility, daily observation records, continuous visibility windows, and side-by-side site comparisons.

By combining lunar terrain with time-dependent celestial geometry, LUNA-RESOLVE provides a visual decision-support tool for comparing environmental conditions at potential exploration locations. It also makes its modeling assumptions and limitations explicit: geometric visibility alone does not guarantee usable power or communications availability.
details:
LUNA-RESOLVE is a scientific analysis and visualization platform designed to explore environmental conditions at candidate lunar south-pole landing regions. The project focuses on two important factors for surface exploration: direct solar illumination and geometric visibility of Earth.

The scientific workflow combines NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation products with SPICE-based celestial geometry. It processes local terrain elevation data to derive horizon profiles and evaluates solar elevation and azimuth against those terrain horizons. Earth visibility is modeled as an apparent disk and classified as fully visible, partially visible, or not visible.

We analyzed Nobile Rim 1 and Connecting Ridge over a 30-day period, from 14 November to 13 December 2026. Each site has 1,441 observations sampled at 30-minute intervals. Nobile Rim 1 also includes observer-height scenarios at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, and 5 metres.

The web dashboard presents mission snapshots, interactive elevation charts, date-based observation tables, visibility timelines, continuous visibility windows, and side-by-side site comparisons. It allows users to inspect individual observations and understand how local terrain influences visibility over time.

The technology stack includes Python, SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, SciPy, PyProj, React, JavaScript, and Vite. The frontend is deployed publicly through Vercel, while the scientific processing workflow generates the datasets consumed by the dashboard.

The project's key contribution is combining terrain-aware visibility analysis, observer-height scenarios, time-dependent celestial geometry, and interactive exploration in one platform. It is intended as a comparative decision-support prototype for lunar mission-environment exploration, not as a landing-site certification or operational power and communications prediction system.

The team considered terrain resolution, interpolation, observer height, sampling interval, celestial geometry, and uncertainty when interpreting results. The dashboard explicitly documents these assumptions and the limitations of geometric visibility models.
